This constellation is considered pathognomonic in the appropriate clinical context. Follicular lymphoma grade 1 may mimic this architecture but typically shows neoplastic follicles lacking regression and lacks the dramatic capillary proliferation and mantle zone concentricity. Reactive hyperplasia can show some overlap but rarely demonstrates such pronounced regressed follicles with organized mantle layers and capillary proliferation. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma may show expanded follicles with LP cells, but lacks the classic hyaline-vascular features and usually has less prominent interfollicular capillaries. IgG4-related disease can cause lymphadenopathy and lymphoid expansion, but it is defined by IgG4+ plasma cell infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis—not the described histology; Dutcher bodies or amyloid would argue against it, and their absence here lowers likelihood. Confidence scores reflect histologic specificity: hyaline-vascular Castleman is the best fit (0.92); others are downgraded based on architectural fidelity, immunophenotypic expectations, and frequency of misclassification."}

The diagnostic questions posed strongly suggest histopathologic evaluation is underway and center on classic features of Castleman disease: regressed germinal centers with concentric 'onion-skin' lymphocytic mantles and prominent interfollicular capillary proliferation are hallmark findings of hyaline-vascular Castleman disease (HVCD), making it the most likely diagnosis (confidence 0.92). Follicular lymphoma grade 1 shares overlapping features (e.g., well-formed follicles), but typically lacks the dramatic vascular proliferation and mantle zone hyperplasia of HVCD; however, low-grade FL remains plausible (0.78). Reactive hyperplasia can mimic HVCD but usually preserves tingible body macrophages and lacks regressed germinal centers with hyalinized vessels—hence moderate likelihood (0.65). Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma may show expanded follicles with LP cells, but lacks the characteristic capillary proliferation and concentric lamination, lowering confidence (0.58). IgG4-related lymphadenopathy often shows storiform fibrosis and IgG4+ plasma cells, but Dutcher bodies and amyloid are not typical; absence of reported IgG4 staining or storiform pattern reduces plausibility (0.42). Diagnostic uncertainty is high due to overlapping morphology and lack of definitive ancillary test results (e.g., immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, IgG4 quantification)."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Hyalinizing Follicular Lymphoma", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Castleman Disease, Hyaline-Vascular Type", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Follicular Dendritic Cell Sarcoma", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Nodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma", "confidence": 0.62}, {"diagnosis": "Progressive Transformation of Germinal Centers", "confidence": 0.58}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The clinical presentation—a painless, persistent (3-month) cervical lymphadenopathy—raises concern for indolent lymphoproliferative or reactive nodal processes. The diagnostic questions posed strongly suggest histopathologic evaluation is underway and focus on features characteristic of hyalinizing/follicular-patterned disorders: regressed germinal centers with concentric lymphocytes (onion-skinning), interfollicular capillary proliferation, Dutcher bodies/amyloid (suggesting plasma cell dyscrasia or chronic antigenic stimulation), and BCL2 expression in germinal centers (aberrant in normal follicles but typical in hyalinizing follicular lymphoma and hyaline-vascular Castleman disease). Hyalinizing Follicular Lymphoma (HFL) is the top consideration because it uniquely combines regressed germinal centers, prominent mantle zones, capillary proliferation, and strong BCL2+ germinal center B-cells—distinguishing it from conventional follicular lymphoma. Castleman disease, hyaline-vascular type, is highly plausible given identical architectural features (onion-skinning, capillary tufts, hypervascular interfollicular zones) and frequent BCL2+ germinal centers; however, it lacks neoplastic B-cell clonality and typically shows polyclonal plasma cells without Dutcher bodies. FDC sarcoma is less common but can mimic hyalinized follicular patterns and may show scattered BCL2+ cells, though it’s usually BCL2-negative in tumor cells and expresses CD21/CD23. NMZL may present with similar morphology but typically lacks prominent capillary proliferation and shows marginal zone expansion rather than regressed follicles with mantle zone accentuation. PTGC is a benign reactive process with enlarged, transformed follicles—not regressed—and lacks sclerosis or capillary proliferation; its inclusion reflects low-confidence overlap in early descriptions but is increasingly recognized as distinct from true hyalinizing lesions. Confidence scores reflect relative frequency, histomorphologic specificity of the queried features, and immunophenotypic alignment."}
